subject: Chemistry
title: Iron, Nitrogen and an Electron Ferry: Why Transition Metals Are Good Catalysts
summary: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up by lowering its activation energy. Transition metals are good catalysts because they can adopt multiple oxidation states and form complexes. On a metal surface (iron in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process, nickel in hydrogenation) reactant molecules bond to surface atoms using 3d and 4s electrons, so their concentration rises and their bonds weaken. In solution, Fe³⁺ ferries electrons between I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻ (2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂; 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻) and is regenerated.

notes.title: 12 – Catalytic Properties: Why Transition Metals Are Good Catalysts

keyPoints: A **catalyst** speeds up a reaction and is **not used up**: it lowers the **activation energy**.
At a **surface**, reactants bond to metal atoms (**3d + 4s electrons**): their **concentration rises** and their **bonds weaken**.
**Fe** (Haber), **V₂O₅** (Contact) and **Ni** (hydrogenation of oils) are industrial transition-metal catalysts.
**Fe³⁺ ⇄ Fe²⁺** ferries electrons between I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻ (two repelling anions) and comes back unchanged.

blocks.p: 2I⁻ + S₂O₈²⁻ → I₂ + 2SO₄²⁻ is slow: both are negative and repel. With Fe³⁺: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, then 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻. Adding the steps, Fe³⁺ cancels: it is a catalyst. E°: +0.54 V (I₂/I⁻) < +0.77 V (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) < +2.01 V (S₂O₈²⁻/SO₄²⁻), so both steps are feasible.

quiz.q: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by:
quiz.explain: It provides a path of lower Eₐ and is regenerated.
